Hi Maik,

Sorry for the delay. There were a number of issues here, now addressed in the GitHub version of the package, which you can install via  devtools::install_github("ctmm-initiative/ctmm")
This particular error came from the default argument fast=TRUE failing in speed(). fast=TRUE invokes the CLT and one of your parameter estimates (a location variance) was on a boundary. I have now included a stop() message to inform users when this happens, so that they can switch to fast=FALSE.
The collapsed variance estimate (no motion along the short axis of the distribution) appears very exacerbated by using AIC on such small sample sizes. AIC/BIC is not really reliable on samples this small. The better alternative for speed/distance estimation is probably "LOOCV", but with 24 data points, this is going to run 24 times slower. With a different dataset, you might also try IC=NA,MSPE='velocity', but without always picking up velocity continuity, I suspect this will not be reliable here.
The way I had things coded, with a collapsing location variance parameter estimate and bad initial guess on its orientation, the optimizer could get stuck. I restructured this code so that this can't happen. However, if you are simultaneously estimating location error (rather than using calibration data or a plausible guess), then I can foresee a scenario where the optimizer can get stuck if both location variances collapse and all variance is explained by location error.
With my limited testing, the simultaneously estimated location error estimates were all over the place and not trustworthy. I would, instead, fix the error estimates and see what the sensitivity is.
Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ushma,

If you plot the two objects, you can see that they look different (Gaussian versus KDE) and should have different areas. The Gaussian estimate assumes a particular model, but has better statistical efficiency. If the data are not Gaussian, then the Gaussian estimate is just estimating variance, which is still meaningful, but is not exactly area.

If you have larger effective sample sizes and are interested in areas, then you want AKDE. If you have smaller effective sample sizes and are willing to suffice with a proxy for area, then you might consider the Gaussian estimates.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
De nada Martin,

PDF: probability density function, which is >=0 and integrates to 1. Its values are continuous probability densities for the point location.
PMF: probability mass function, which is >=0 and sums to 1. Its values are discrete probability mass for the cell.
CDF: cumulative distribution function, which ranges from 0 to 1. Its values are HDR quantiles here in 2D.

It only makes sense to average the PDF/PMF. If you average CDFs, then you likely will not end up with a mathematically valid CDF. When you average PDF/PMF, then it has the meaning of a mixture distribution, where the weights are the proportion of time spent in each constituent distribution.

Best,
Chris

Chris

messages.subject_clean: Parameterizing OU and OUf's sigma and tau
messages.body_plain:
Hi Meredith,

The sigma parameter in the OU, OUf, and OUF models is indeed the asymptote of the variogram. The tau parameter in OU and OUf are different. In the OU model, there is a tau[position] parameter that is the timescale over which autocorrelation in location decays. This can be thought of as the home-range crossing timescale. In the OUF model, there is an additional tau[velocity] parameter that is the timescale over which autocorrelation in velocity decays. This can be thought of as the persistence of motion timescale. In the OUf model, the tau[position] and tau[velocity] parameters cannot be distinguished and only one parameter is estimated. So in this model, the animal is almost bee-lining back and forth across its home range. The ctmm.guess() function should be able to provide reasonable initial guesstimates for the parameters, as long as severe data quality isn't an issue. There should rarely be the need to do manual tinkering, especially as I have been improving ctmm's optimizer. Initial guesses usually only need to be in the ballpark for fitting.

I have some notes on what can slow down bandwidth/weight optimization with in help('bandwidth'). Those notes are updated in the development branch of ctmm on GitHub, which I have copied below. akde() calls bandwidth() when running and passes any arguments provided. You do not need to call bandwidth() directly in normal operation.

Best,
Chris

> fast=TRUE grids the data with grid width dt and applies FFT algorithms, for a computational cost as low as O(n \log n) with only O(n) function evaluations. If no dt is specified, the minimum sampling interval min(diff(data$t)) is used. If the data are irregular (permitting gaps), then dt may need to be several times smaller to avoid slow down. In this case, try setting trace=TRUE and decreasing dt until the interations speed up and the number of feasibility assessments becomes less than O(n). On the other hand, if the data contain some very tiny time intervals, say 1 second among hourly sampled data, then the default dt setting will create an excessively high-resolution discretization of time, which will also cause slowdown. In this case CTMM should contain an error model and dt can likely be increased to a larger fraction of the median sampling interval.
>
> fast=FALSE uses exact times and has a computational cost as low as O(n^2), including O(n^2) function evaluations. With PC="direct" this method will produce a result that is exact to within machine precision, but with a computational cost of O(n^3). fast=FALSE,PC='direct' is often the fastest method with small datasets, where n ≤ O(1,000), but scales terribly with larger datasets.
